title: One shared browser connection

findings.point: Root cause of the user's literal complaint: the Brain can't send work to an agent that already exists. Its only actions are none, start_agent, draft_reply and open. A delegation request therefore becomes start_agent, which creates a fresh agent with no tab. In Brave mode that agent is told it may only use tabs it opens or tabs the user hands it, so it asks for a tab. Messaging an agent already works through the 'send' socket message, but the Brain never uses it.

design:
ONE SHARED DEBUGGING CONNECTION: a CDP relay inside `ai-browser app`

0. Shape
- New module app/cdprelay.py (Relay, Upstream, Client). BraveLink owns the only websocket to Brave: BraveLink.connect() opens the upstream, and that is the only thing that ever asks "Allow remote debugging?". TabWatch becomes an in-process, privileged client of the relay with no websocket of its own.
- Endpoint: WebSocketRoute("/cdp") on the existing AppServer (server.py:202-210), 127.0.0.1 only. Clients speak plain CDP JSON, so Browser, live view and QA code stay unchanged.
- Engine: _start_chrome("chrome") (engine.py:182-198) uses the relay when one is available and the direct path otherwise. CDP.connect (cdp.py:36-38) gains a headers argument.

1. CDP multiplexing
- Id remapping: the relay keeps one upstream id counter. pending[U] = (client, client's id, method, params). A response gets the client's id back, is post-processed (createTarget records the owner, attachToTarget binds the session, getTargets is filtered) and goes only to that client. When the upstream drops, every pending command fails with error -32000 "browser connection lost".
- Flattened sessionId routing: attachToTarget without flatten:true is refused. The sessionId from the attach response binds to the client. In flatten mode Chrome sends Target.attachedToTarget, and possibly the session's first events, before that response, so events for an unknown sessionId wait in a small buffer (about 2 s, 256 messages) and are released to the client once the response binds it. Child sessions (attachedToTarget with a parent sessionId) inherit the parent's owner. detachedFromTarget is routed, then the binding is dropped. A command on a session the client doesn't own gets -32001 "Session with given id not found".
- Per-client event filtering: session events go to the session's owner only. Browser-level Target.targetCreated, targetInfoChanged, targetDestroyed and targetCrashed go only to clients that turned discovery on, and only for targets visible to them. Visible means own, handed, or a popup whose openerId is an own target. The user's own tabs' titles and URLs no longer reach agents at all. Other browser-level events go to the app only; Inspector.detached goes to everyone.
- Target.setDiscoverTargets per client: the relay turns discovery on upstream once, at connect (as tabs.py:35 does now). A client's {discover:true} only flips a per-client flag: the relay replies {} and sends synthetic targetCreated events for the visible targets in its cache. {discover:false} turns the flag off.
- Target.setAutoAttach per client: refused at browser level. Browser-level auto-attach would attach to, and with waitForDebuggerOnStart pause, every new tab including the user's. Allowed at session level (iframes and workers of an own page); the child sessions belong to the parent's owner.
- Browser-level commands: allowlist only.
  - Target.createTarget: the caller becomes the owner. In Brave mode the relay forces background:true and allows only http, https, about:blank and data: URLs. The tab's browserContextId is recorded, and the relay warns if an agent's tabs land in two different profiles.
  - attachToTarget, activateTarget, getTargetInfo: own or handed targets.
  - closeTarget: own targets only. Handed tabs can be detached, never closed.
  - detachFromTarget: own sessions.
  - getTargets: filtered to visible targets.
  - Browser.getVersion: allowed.
  - Browser.cancelDownload: only for download guids seen in Page.downloadWillBegin on the client's own sessions.
  - Everything else at browser level is refused: Browser.close, crash, setDownloadBehavior, grantPermissions, setPermission; Target.exposeDevToolsProtocol, create/disposeBrowserContext; Storage.*, SystemInfo.*, Tethering.*.
  - Session level is allowed except whole-profile cookie calls (Network.getAllCookies, Storage.*Cookies) and Page.navigate to a scheme outside the list. This backs up browser.py's url_problem check.
- Backpressure: each client gets a bounded outbound queue. On overflow (screenshots, screencast frames) that one client is closed; the upstream never stalls.
- Client goes away: the upstream stays open, so Chrome will not clean up for it. The relay sends Target.detachFromTarget for every session the client owned, which ends its focus emulation, scripts and Network buffers on those tabs. Tabs stay open: the app closes an agent's tabs when the agent closes (agents.py:191-209). A Claude Code session's own unhanded tabs are closed if it hasn't come back within a grace period (about 60 s).

2. Ownership: enforce it in the relay (recommended: yes)
- Identity comes from the token, not the connection:
  - Agents: a token per agent, minted in AgentManager.create (agents.py:141-147). It replaces the shared agent_token (server.py:148).
  - Claude Code sessions: link.json's session token only buys /agent-hello, which returns a per-session relay token.
- What a client may use:
  - Own: targets it created through the relay, popups its own tabs opened, and their child sessions.
  - Handed: agent.adopted, set by Hand over and cleared by Take back.
- The relay's table becomes the app's truth for owners. It feeds BraveLink._owners directly instead of trusting /agent-events and /agent-claim self-reports (server.py:281-300, 362-371, 408-429).
- Take back detaches the agent's session on that tab immediately (today there is a window of up to 1 s: agentlink.py:68-81; engine.py:271-280).
- Ownership survives an engine reconnect (New chat), so an agent keeps its tabs.
- The app's internal client stays privileged: thumbnails and text of READABLE tabs (bravelink.py:22, 160-182), Watch for any tab on the user's click, closing agent tabs.

3. Token-protected endpoint
- Address ws://127.0.0.1:<app port>/cdp. The token travels in the X-AIB-Agent-Token handshake header, never the query string, and is checked with hmac.compare_digest.
- Refuse any handshake that carries an Origin header (web pages always send one, our client doesn't) or a Host other than 127.0.0.1:<port>, which blocks DNS rebinding. Close code 4403, as in server.py:46.
- Tokens rotate every app run and live only in 0600 files (mcp.json: bridge.py:305; link.json: run.py:110-116).
- Discovery:
  - Agents get AIB_APP_CDP in agents.env (run.py:207-212).
  - Sessions read a "cdp" field in link.json, validated the way _local_events validates (agentlink.py:120-130): ws scheme, 127.0.0.1, path /cdp.

4. When the app isn't running (Claude Code sessions alone)
- The engine tries, in order: the relay from env (agents); the relay from link.json if its pid is alive (sessions); then today's direct connection, which asks once per session process.
- If the app is up but the relay errors, the engine reports the error and never silently goes direct, because a direct connection would ask out of the blue.
- While the app runs, sessions always land in the app's browser (Brave). That fixes "sometimes Chrome", which today comes from chrome.py:55-63.
- Optional later step: `ai-browser relay`, the same module run standalone with its own lock and relay.json. It closes the upstream after about 10 minutes with no clients, so several bare sessions share one Allow.

5. Reconnects
- Upstream states mirror BraveLink: off, ready, asking, connected, refused, lost.
- Upstream drop:
  - Fail all pending commands.
  - Send each client a synthetic detachedFromTarget for each of its sessions.
  - Close all client sockets with code 4410 "browser gone". Engines then take their existing reconnect path (engine.py:383-391), which reconnects to the relay, not to Brave.
- When to reopen the upstream: only right after a user action, the same consent timing as bravelink.py:1-8. That means app start, Connect or Try again, an agent's turn (server.py:174), or a client's first command after the user gave it a task.
  - Reopening is single-flight: every waiting client shares one attempt, so the user sees one question.
  - The wait is 60 s (ALLOW_WAIT).
  - If the user clicks Deny, clients get a clear error and nothing retries on its own.
- Client reconnect: no question, and identity plus ownership are kept.

6. Expected effect, from Chromium's source
- One "Allow remote debugging?" per app run, and once more after each Brave restart. Today it is 1 + N + M, plus one on every engine restart.
- The automation bar appears once per upstream connection. If the user closes it, it stays closed while the connection lives, because Chrome only re-shows it when a connection opens or closes (chrome_devtools_manager_delegate.cc:551-564; devtools_http_handler.cc:924-929, 1050-1057). Nothing hides, closes or clicks it.

7. Effort: about 3-5 developer days, roughly 1,500-2,000 lines including tests
- Relay core: id map, session binding buffer, virtual discovery, allowlist, ownership, queues, upstream state machine. About 600 lines, plus about 700 lines of tests run against a throwaway Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port=0, which needs no Allow and goes through the same code.
- BraveLink and TabWatch moved onto the relay: about 120 lines.
- server.py /cdp route, per-agent and per-session tokens, hello returning a relay token: about 150 lines.
- run.py and agents.py env, link.json "cdp": about 40 lines.
- engine.py, cdp.py, agentlink.py relay-or-direct choice and headers: about 80 lines.
- Spec Decision 12, the SWITCH and AI Home text, and a manual check in the user's Brave.

8. Separate from the relay, but the user's actual complaint: the Brain needs a "send_to_agent" action (agent id plus the user's words, confirmed like start_agent) that calls agents.send. Optionally it could also propose a Hand over of a named tab. With relay ownership, a handed tab is usable at once.
risks: Standing grant. One Allow now covers every holder of a relay token for the whole app run, so any same-user process that can read the 0600 mcp.json or link.json can drive Brave without a new question. It could open a signed-in site in a new tab, even though the relay keeps it off the user's own tabs and blocks cookie APIs. Mitigations: enforce ownership; refuse Origin and odd Host headers; rotate tokens every run; list the relay's clients in AI Home with a Disconnect button; optionally close the upstream after idling.

Consent wording changes. The spec's Decision 12 and run.py:76-84 tell the user to expect a question per agent and to click Deny at other times. The copy must change, or the user may Deny the one question that matters, or later trust prompts that come from somewhere else.

Flatten race. Target.attachedToTarget and early session events can arrive before the attach response. Without the binding buffer, events get misrouted or dropped. Two clients attaching to the same tab (an app thumbnail and the agent) create two separate upstream sessions, which is allowed but must be tested.

One socket carries everything. Head-of-line blocking and JSON re-parsing of large screenshot and screencast frames run through Python. A slow client must be cut off, not allowed to stall the upstream.

Single point of failure. If the app crashes or restarts, every agent and session loses the browser at once. Engines must reconnect cleanly, and sessions must not silently fall back to direct connections, which would ask out of the blue.
Allowlist drift. A new CDP call in browser.py, live.py or qa/ fails through the relay until it is added. CI should run the engine's browser tests through the relay against a throwaway Chrome.
Out of the relay's reach. Other tools in a session (chrome-devtools-mcp --autoConnect, Playwright connectOverCDP) still open their own connections, which ask again and re-show the bar.

Multi-profile. CDP only creates tabs in the last-used regular profile (chrome_target_handler.cc:110-121; devtools_browser_context_manager.cc:66-77). The relay can detect stray tabs but can't pin a profile.

Evidence gap. The question count and the bar behaviour come from Chromium main and Brave's patch list. The headless probe confirmed approval mode and pending per-connection handshakes, but no dialog or bar was counted in a real Brave 152. The user needs to check this by hand: two agents, one question; close the bar, start a second agent, the bar stays closed.

Ownership enforcement could break flows that rely on today's looser rules: popups opened outside an act step, the Train form's picked page, Brain-marked tabs. These must map to explicit grants from the app.
open_questions_for_user: When you ask the Brain to give work to an agent that's already running, should it send your words to that agent and offer to hand it a tab, instead of starting a new one? Today it can only start a new agent or open one.

While AI Browser is running, should Claude Code sessions use the app's single connection to Brave? That means one Allow in total, always Brave, never Chrome. Or should they keep connecting on their own?

When the app isn't running, is one Allow per Claude Code session acceptable (today's behaviour)? Or would you like a small background helper that holds Brave's connection for about 10 minutes after the last use?

Should the app hold Brave's connection for its whole run? The automation bar would then stay closed once you close it, but any program on this computer that can read AI Browser's token files could use Brave without asking. Or should it drop the connection after some idle minutes, so you get one more Allow next time?

You use several Brave profiles. Browser automation can only open tabs in the profile you used last. Should agents stop and tell you when their tab lands in a different profile from the one they started in?

design:
GOAL
Turn AI Browser's UI (AI Home, Mission Control, the Brain) into one app window. It is served over http by the app server and shown in an --app window of an installed Chromium, on its own profile, with no debugging flag. That means no tabs, no address bar, no "Allow remote debugging?" prompt, no automation bar, and navigator.webdriver false (all measured). The user no longer loads the AI Browser extension by hand: only Brave's watcher stays an extension. Below, "app mode" means Chrome's --app window, not the engine's AIB_BROWSER=app.

1. SERVING THE PAGES (app/server.py)
- Move app/extension/* (minus manifest.json and worker.js) to app/ui/. Serve it with Starlette static routes: /home (home.html), /mission, /brain (a full Brain page: inbox, watch list, style notes and permission cards, built from brainui.js), and the .js/.css assets by name. Send Cache-Control: no-store, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.
- Every page gets this Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' ws://127.0.0.1:<port>; img-src 'self' data: blob:; media-src 'self' blob:; worker-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'; object-src 'none'. This replaces MV3's default extension CSP. Thumbnails are data: JPEGs, and pages keep setting text with textContent only.
- Host check on every HTTP and WS route: only 127.0.0.1:<port> (TrustedHost, or a small middleware). This blocks DNS rebinding, which matters because /setup embeds the setup key.

2. HOW THE PAGE GETS AUTHENTICATED (no token in a lasting URL, no token readable by JS)
- At each start the server makes ui_secret (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)). Before each window launch it makes a one-time launch_code: single use, valid 60 s.
- The launcher opens --app=http://127.0.0.1:<port>/open?code=<launch_code>. GET /open checks and consumes the code with hmac.compare_digest. It then answers 303 → /home with: Set-Cookie: aib_ui_<port>=<ui_secret>; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/ (and Secure, which Chrome accepts on 127.0.0.1, as measured). It sets no Max-Age, so the cookie lives only for the session. The redirect drops the code from the window's URL and history. This is the same pattern Jupyter uses.
- A /ws upgrade from a page is accepted only when all of these hold: Origin is exactly http://127.0.0.1:<port>, Host is 127.0.0.1:<port>, and the cookie matches ui_secret. The existing ?token= + chrome-extension:// path stays for Brave's watcher only. In _origin_of, the http origin counts as "AI Browser's own page" wherever the code now tests "not the watcher's origin" (HEARING, TALK and BRAVE messages).
- A page opened without the cookie (for example http://127.0.0.1:8792/home typed into Brave, or opened by an agent driving Brave) gets the HTML and a refused socket. It shows "Open AI Browser from the app". The cookie lives only in the app window's own profile, so agents in Brave can never reach the UI socket.
- Cookies for 127.0.0.1 go to every port (measured), so the app profile must never load third-party local pages (see external links below). The cookie name carries the port.
- link.js: in an extension page (location.protocol === 'chrome-extension:'), keep the config.json + ?token path for the watcher. On http, connect with new WebSocket(`ws://${location.host}/ws`), with no token.

3. REPLACING EACH chrome.* USE
- runtime.getURL('config.json') (link.js:19, home.js:258, brainui.js:41): use location.origin. The setup links become '/setup#switch' and '/setup#brave'.
- runtime.getURL('home.html' / 'mission.html'): use '/home' and '/mission' as same-window navigation. mission.html:20 already uses a plain link back. For a second window, use window.open('/mission', 'aib-mission', 'popup,width=1280,height=860'). The popup feature keeps it app-like (measured B4); plain _blank would open a tabbed window (measured B2/B3).
- runtime.getURL('mic-worklet.js') (mic.js:13): new URL('./mic-worklet.js', import.meta.url). Measured working over http (A4).
- storage.local 'model' and 'voice': move to server-side prefs (a 'prefs' / 'prefs_set' message, saved in <home>/app/prefs.json). This survives a port change (the origin changes with it) and is shared with the watcher's side chat in Brave, which has a different origin. If simpler, use localStorage inside try/catch only as a cache.
- tabs.* and windows.* in home.js: openMission and the pin logic (home.js:557-565) go. The browser card's "Show me how" opens /setup#switch in the same window or as a popup. Watch, Hand over and Take back already go through the server.
- tabs.*, tabGroups.*, debugger.getTargets, sidePanel, action badge, commands (worker.js, panel.js, link.js:70-84) leave the app pages. With AI Browser's own tabs gone, its tab groups go too: Brave's watcher already groups agent tabs (worker.js:110-119 braveMode). The side panel (panel.*) moves into the watcher, as already approved for "Side chat into the watcher extension". Its Brave-mode branch never needs debugger.getTargets.
- Badge: set document.title to '(n) AI Home' and call navigator.setAppBadge(n). setAppBadge exists and resolved in the probe (A4), but whether the Dock shows it for a non-installed --app window was not checked. The watcher's action badge and notifications in Brave already get permission_request and check_request (server.py:625-626).
- omnibox 'ai' (worker.js:169-170): an app window has no address bar. Move the keyword into the watcher's manifest (Brave is where the user types URLs). The watcher's worker sends new_task / workflow_run over its socket, which the server accepts today (server.py:681 is not gated by origin). The app window keeps its task boxes. A Cmd/Ctrl+K command bar in the window is optional.
- runtime.onInstalled/onStartup and the newtab override: nothing replaces them. The launcher opens /home itself.
- External links (check.js:32 live view; any link to a site): the live view (our own 127.0.0.1:877x page) opens with window.open(live, 'aib-live', 'popup,noopener,width=1280,height=860'). Real websites go to the user's browser: a new 'open_url' message (http/https only) → BraveLink opens a tab in Brave when connected, else the OS default browser. The app window never navigates away from its own origin.

4. LAUNCHING THE WINDOW (new app/window.py, replacing launch_app_browser in run.py:201)
- Command line: <binary> --user-data-dir=<home>/app/window --app=http://127.0.0.1:<port>/open?code=… --no-first-run --no-default-browser-check --disable-search-engine-choice-screen --window-size=1440,960, and optionally --autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required (see question). It has NO --remote-debugging-port, NO --remote-debugging-pipe, NO --enable-automation and NO --load-extension. Use a plain Popen or posix_spawn.
- Which binary ("App window browser" in Settings: Auto / Chrome / Brave / Edge, changeable any time):
  - Mac: Auto prefers an installed Chromium that is not the user's everyday browser (Chrome when they use Brave). Then the user's Brave and the app window never share an app bundle (see risks). Otherwise Brave on its own profile.
  - Windows: Edge first (always installed), then Chrome, then Brave. platforms.browser_candidates needs an 'edge' entry: Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe, plus the msedge.exe App Paths registry key.
- The app-window profile (<home>/app/window) is never AI Browser's old <home>/browser and never the user's profile. It never has a DevToolsActivePort, so no engine and no other process can drive it.
- Lifetime: the app ends when the window closes, as today. Since macOS keeps the process alive with no window (measured A2), use the window's socket. When no http-origin socket has been connected for WINDOW_GRACE ≈ 3 s (a reload reconnects in milliseconds), the app stops and terminates the browser process it started, which is safe on our own profile. On Windows, or when the user presses Cmd+Q, process exit also ends it, as in run.py:248.
- Single instance: the existing lock (run.py:130) refuses a second run. When a socket is already connected, a "Show" request from the CLI just has the page call window.focus(). Otherwise it relaunches with a fresh code.

5. TABWATCH, AI BROWSER'S TABS, AND AGENTS THAT USED AI BROWSER'S CHROME
- TabWatch on AI Browser (run.py:217-221) goes away. The TabWatch class stays, because BraveLink uses it for the user's Brave. AI Home's Tabs list shows Brave's tabs (server.attach_brave already does this).
- The engine's 'app' mode (bridge.py:297, engine.py:186-214) loses its browser. Either retire it (agents browse in the browser chosen in Settings, else the Docker sandbox), or keep an opt-in "Separate agent browser": the old Chrome on <home>/browser with --remote-debugging-port=0, no extension and no tab groups, started lazily when an agent first needs it. That browser is the automated one (webdriver true, Google sign-in refused). Either way, pass AIB_APP_ORIGIN to engines so url_problem refuses http://127.0.0.1:<app port>/, as it refuses chrome-extension:// today.
- The setup flow for AI Browser's own extension goes away: setup_text, chrome://extensions, prepare_extension, extension_installed, the origin-mismatch message for AI Browser (run.py:55-63,222-229; server.py:185-194). /setup keeps only Brave's watcher and the switch steps.

6. VOICE, MIC AND WEBGL IN THE APP WINDOW
- WebGL 1 and 2 are hardware-accelerated in Chrome and Brave app windows (ANGLE Metal on this Mac), so blob.js:427 and scene.js are unchanged.
- getUserMedia: 127.0.0.1 is a secure context. The site prompt appears in the app window (measured 'prompt' → pending). talk.js's explain card (talk.js:233-256) still fits: Chrome's "Allow while visiting the site" is remembered per origin in <home>/app/window, so keep the port stable (try the last port first and save it in <home>/app/port). macOS also asks once per browser app. If Chrome hosts the window and was never given the mic, macOS shows its own prompt. talk.js's micProblem already words the System Settings fix.
- speechSynthesis: the voices are there (Chrome 199, of them 180 local; Brave 181 local). Without a click, speak() is refused (not-allowed). voice.js already asks for a click. With --autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required on our own app window it speaks at once (measured A3). This flag only changes autoplay inside our own app profile; it does not disguise anything.
- AudioContext for the mic starts on the user's press (mic.js), so the autoplay policy does not block it.

7. LATER: PACKAGING AS A DOUBLE-CLICK APP (note only)
- Mac: a small "AI Browser.app" launcher (a shell or PyInstaller stub, LSUIElement so it has no Dock icon of its own) that runs `ai-browser app`. The visible window is still Chrome's, Brave's or Edge's process, so the Dock and menu bar show that browser's name and icon. A real app identity needs one of two things: Chrome's own "Install app" (a web app manifest at a fixed origin/port, which the user installs once; it then gets an app shim with its own Dock icon and launches with --app-id), or a native shell (pywebview on WKWebView/WebView2). A native shell has to recheck mic entitlements, AudioWorklet and speech.
- PyInstaller has to bundle uvicorn, starlette, websockets and the Whisper engine. The claude CLI stays a separate install. It needs signing and notarization (Gatekeeper; SmartScreen on Windows).

8. EFFORT (about 5 to 7 days)
- Server (static routes, CSP, Host check, /open + cookie, socket auth, prefs): 1 day.
- app/window.py (browser choice for Mac and Windows, launch, lifetime, focus) and the run.py rewrite: 1 day.
- UI JS port (link.js with both modes, home.js, mission.js, mic.js, brainui.js, check.js, a new /brain page; delete worker.js; omnibox and badge to the watcher): 1 to 1.5 days.
- Removing the extension setup and deciding the engine's 'app' mode: 0.5 to 1 day.
- Tests: 1.5 to 2 days, broken down below.

9. WHAT THE TESTS NEED
- `stack` (test_home.py:46-93): start a throwaway headless Chrome with no extension (conftest's throwaway_chrome / chrome_browser pattern, conftest.py:73-105) and open f"{url}/open?code={server.new_launch_code()}". Tests may keep CDP on this throwaway: only the product's window never has a port.
- open_page targets change from chrome-extension://{id}/home.html to {url}/home (test_home, test_mission.open_mission, test_ai_home_phase2, test_brain_ui, test_check_card, test_talk, test_mission_visuals). Replace runtime.getURL('x.js') imports with '/x.js' (test_mission_visuals.py:20,399,602; test_talk.py:37,182,194,553). Mic tests grant audioCapture with CDP Browser.grantPermissions and use fake-device flags.
- worker_js tests for AI Browser's tab groups, pinned AI Home and the omnibox (test_home.py:112-242, 6 uses; test_ai_home_phase2 1; test_workflows 2) are deleted or move to test_watcher / test_watcher_groups if the keyword moves there.
- test_panel (5) moves to the watcher tests. test_appbrowser (17) is mostly replaced by test_appwindow: the command line has no debugging flag, browser choice per OS, lifetime, and the one-time code. test_app_run (16) is rewritten for the window launch and socket lifetime. test_app_server gains cookie/origin/host tests: a wrong Origin, a missing cookie, a reused or expired code, a foreign Host, and the watcher's token path unchanged. test_appmode (15) follows the 'app'-mode decision.
- Bonus: `stack` no longer needs the DevTools pipe, so these UI tests can drop out of PIPE_FIXTURES and run on Windows.

10. RELATED: THE USER'S DELEGATION COMPLAINT (fix belongs to the Brain topic, noted here because Mission Control's talk lives in this window)
- Add a closed action 'tell_agent' {agent: <known id>} to brain/talk.py ACTIONS and the prompt. It works like start_agent: a proposal card "Send to <agent name>: <the user's own words>", which runs only on Send or a plain yes, through agents.send(agent_id, words). parse_answer already checks agent ids for 'open'. The prompt should prefer tell_agent when the user names or refers to an existing agent. A Brain-started agent in Brave should be told it may open its own tab ('open url'), rather than waiting for one to be handed over.
risks: With window.open/_blank, Cmd+N or Cmd+T, the user gets a normal tabbed browser window in the app profile (measured B2/B3), and the browser look returns. Every link the code opens must use popup features or go to the user's browser. The user can still open one by hand.

Cookies on 127.0.0.1 are shared across ports (measured), so the UI cookie reaches any local server the app window requests. The app profile must never load third-party local pages, such as a dev server the user is QA-ing.

macOS keeps the browser process alive after the window closes (measured A2). Without socket-based lifetime and terminating the process, a windowless Chrome or Brave stays in the Dock and the app never ends.

The origin includes the port. If 8792 is taken (the user's running app already uses 8792/8793), the origin changes: localStorage, the saved mic permission and any future installed-app identity reset. The fix is server-side prefs plus a remembered port.

If the app window runs on the same browser as the user's everyday Brave, the Dock shows two Brave icons. macOS may also deliver links clicked in other apps to the app-window instance (not measured, to avoid touching the user's real browsers). Hosting it on Chrome avoids that, but the Dock then shows Chrome, which the user may read as 'Chrome instead of Brave'.

macOS asks for the microphone once per browser app. If Chrome hosts the window and was never given the mic, a system prompt appears on first talk. In my probe with the site permission granted, getUserMedia waited 8 s, which fits that prompt. The user may have seen a macOS 'Google Chrome would like to access the microphone' dialog during this probe; Don't Allow is fine.

Without a click, speechSynthesis is refused in both Chrome and Brave app windows (measured). Mission Control's remembered Voice-on stays silent until a click unless the window gets --autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required.

Brand identity: the Dock, Cmd-Tab and the menu bar show Chrome, Brave or Edge, with their History and Bookmarks menus, not 'AI Browser'. Only an installed web app (Chrome's app shim) or a native shell fixes that.

Retiring AI Browser's own Chrome removes the engine's 'app' mode. Agents then need the user's browser switch on, the Docker sandbox, or an opt-in separate agent Chrome, which is automated and refuses Google sign-in.
There is no Host-header check today. Once the UI is served over http, DNS rebinding could read /setup (which embeds the setup key) unless Host is pinned to 127.0.0.1:<port>.
link.js, brainui.js and permission.js are shared with Brave's watcher (brain/watcher.py:20). A change that drops the config.json/token path breaks the watcher.

Not verified: Edge's first run on a fresh --user-data-dir and the --app window behaviour on Windows (no Edge on this Mac). In-window navigation to another origin was inconclusive, because the only measurement (B5) also had the automation bar. Whether navigator.setAppBadge shows anything for a non-installed --app window was not checked either.
open_questions_for_user: On your Mac, should AI Browser's app window run on Google Chrome (kept apart from your everyday Brave, no link mix-ups, but the Dock shows a Chrome icon) or on Brave with its own profile (a second Brave icon; links from other apps might land in it)?

With the app window having no debugging port, agents can no longer browse in AI Browser's own Chrome. Should that option be dropped (agents use your Brave or the sandbox), or kept as an opt-in 'separate agent browser'? That one shows the automation bar and Google refuses sign-in there.

May the app window start with --autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required, so Mission Control's voice speaks updates without a click after each start? It only applies to AI Browser's own window profile.

The 'ai' address-bar keyword can't live in an app window, which has no address bar. Move it to the watcher in Brave (type ai + space in Brave's address bar), or drop it in favour of the task box and a Cmd+K bar in the app window?
When you close the app window, should the whole app stop (as now: agents end too), or keep running in the background with a way to reopen the window?

For your delegation problem: should the Brain get a 'send to an existing agent' action that you confirm with Send or yes, so that 'tell the footer agent to also check the header' goes to that agent instead of starting a new one?

title: Choosing the browser and profile

findings.point: Agents' tabs land in whichever profile window the user clicked last, not in a fixed default profile. Target.createTarget without a browserContextId follows the last-focused profile, so agent tabs spread across the user's profiles. Grouping then fails silently in a profile that has no watcher, because each watcher only sees its own profile's tabs. The spec's claim that tabs open 'in Brave's default profile' is wrong.
findings.evidence: Measured in throwaway Chrome 154 and throwaway Brave 152, each with two profiles (/private/tmp/claude-501/profile-probe/probe2.py, probe3.py). After a Profile 2 tab was activated, createTarget without a context landed in Profile 2, with newWindow:true too. After a Default tab was activated, it landed in Default. Code: browser.py:427-434 and grouping.py:44-50 send no context. The claim is at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-02-everyday-brave-design.md:806-807 and grouping.py:8-9. The watcher looks tabs up with chrome.tabs.query({}) (watcher/groups.js:43-45). Measured: an extension's chrome.tabs.query returned only its own profile's 2 tabs, not the other profile's tab (probe4.py, Brave).

findings.point: CDP cannot open a tab in an arbitrary real profile. Target.getBrowserContexts lists no real profiles, only a defaultBrowserContextId, and that is the last-used profile, so it changes when focus changes. createTarget with a browserContextId succeeds only for the profile that is currently the default. Chrome 154 has no windowId parameter on createTarget, and a windowId passed anyway is silently ignored.
findings.evidence: probe.py and probe2.py output: getBrowserContexts returned {'browserContextIds': [], 'defaultBrowserContextId': X}, and X switched from Default's id to Profile 2's id after Target.activateTarget. createTarget with browserContextId=<the other real profile> returned 'Failed to find browser context with id …' in Chrome 154 and in Brave 152. The /json/protocol createTarget parameters are url, left, top, width, height, windowState, browserContextId, enableBeginFrameControl, newWindow, background, forTab, hidden, focus (no windowId). A createTarget with windowId set to Default's window landed in Profile 2's window.

findings.point: Every page of every profile is visible through the instance's one debugging endpoint. Each page's TargetInfo.browserContextId tells the profiles apart, and Browser.getWindowForTarget works for pages in any profile. So the debugging switch, and one 'Allow' for a connection, covers all profiles of that instance: switching profile inside Brave needs no new Allow prompt, while switching to another browser instance does.
findings.evidence: probe.py (headful run): one ws://…/devtools/browser endpoint listed pages in 2 contexts, and getWindowForTarget returned windows 331719195 and 331719193. There is one DevToolsActivePort per user-data-dir (chrome.py:29-37). A second launch of the same user-data-dir with --profile-directory='Profile 2' handed off to the running instance (exit code 0 after 0.24 s).

findings.point: There is a deterministic way to place a tab in a chosen profile without moving focus: the extension in that profile calls chrome.tabs.create({active:false}). The new tab lands in the extension's own profile even when another profile was used last. The engine then sees it over CDP by its marker URL and can attach to it.
findings.evidence: probe4.py in throwaway Brave 152: the last-used context was 3E81E7 and the extension's context was 9F6061. chrome.tabs.create from the extension worker produced a tab that showed up over CDP as ('about:blank#aib-0123…', '9F6061'). The watcher already opens tabs this way for Brain threads (everyday-brave spec:183-184, watcher/worker.js:339-377). Chrome's docs say tabs.create's 'active' does not affect window focus.

findings.point: Extension workers appear as CDP targets with the browserContextId of their profile. Each profile's Secure Preferences records which unpacked extension paths are loaded there. Together, the app can tell which profile folder holds the watcher, and which runtime context that is, by reading files and listing targets, without opening any tab.
findings.evidence: probe4.py (Brave): service_worker targets 'chrome-extension://plejig…/worker.js' with contexts 9F6061 and 3E81E7. In the throwaway profile, '<profile>/Secure Preferences' → extensions.settings.<id> = {'path': '/private/tmp/claude-501/profile-probe/ext', 'location': 8, 'disable_reasons': []}, and Preferences had no entry. The app already derives the watcher's id from its path (app/run.py:206, extension_id_for(watcher)).

findings.point: Profiles can be listed from <user-data-dir>/Local State without connecting. The keys were measured in both Chrome and Brave. user_name and gaia_name can hold the signed-in email, so they must stay local.
findings.evidence: probe2.py and probe3.py: Local State profile keys ['info_cache', 'last_active_profiles', 'last_used', 'metrics', 'profile_counts_reported', 'profiles_order']. info_cache['Default'] = {name: 'Your Chrome' (Brave: 'Personal'), avatar_icon: 'chrome://theme/IDR_PROFILE_AVATAR_26', is_using_default_name, default_avatar_fill_color, profile_highlight_color (signed ARGB int), is_ephemeral, user_name, gaia_name}; 'Profile 2' → 'Person 1'. Local State was only complete after the browser quit, so it lags a live browser: a new profile may appear late.

findings.point: Private-window tabs are listed on the browser endpoint with their own context, but AI Home's tab list never looks at browserContextId. It therefore shows tabs from private windows and from every other profile as 'you' rows. A context-less createTarget never went into a private window.
findings.evidence: probe5.py: after an --incognito window was opened, getTargets listed pages in two contexts (3E368A for incognito, 0FA31C regular), getBrowserContexts listed neither, and a context-less createTarget landed in 0FA31C. The tab list is app/tabs.py:65-69 and 80-84 (keeps only target, url and title) and app/bravelink.py:122-133 (web pages of any context become 'you').

findings.point: 'Running' and 'switch on' can be detected without a debugging session, but both files go stale. DevToolsActivePort and SingletonLock (a symlink to host-pid) stay behind after the browser exits, so the check needs SingletonLock's pid plus a TCP check of the port. Never a websocket.
findings.evidence: lockprobe2 (headless Chrome 154, SIGTERM): after the process exited, DevToolsActivePort, SingletonLock -> 'Kurls-Macbook.local-23735', SingletonSocket and SingletonCookie were all still present. The existing check is TCP-only (chrome.py:40-52). platforms.pid_alive exists (platforms.py:175-187).

findings.point: The user's own setup matches the multiple-profiles complaint: Brave has two profiles and its switch file. Chrome has one profile and no switch file. The macOS default browser is Brave. I read only folder names, file existence and the http/https handler, and opened no connection.
findings.evidence: ~/Library/Application Support/BraveSoftware/Brave-Browser contains Default, 'Profile 1' and DevToolsActivePort. ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome contains Default and no DevToolsActivePort. ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.LaunchServices/com.apple.launchservices.secure.plist maps https/http/public.html to com.brave.browser.

findings.point: Detection must key off the installed app, not the data folder. design:
BROWSER AND PROFILE CHOICE: design

0. Principles
- Detection uses file reads plus a TCP check, never a websocket. It cannot cause an 'Allow remote debugging?' prompt.
- One choice is saved for agents: a browser instance (a user-data-dir) and one profile folder inside it. Every new agent, Brain-started agent and Claude Code session uses it.
- An agent keeps the browser and profile it started in for its whole life. A switch affects only new work.
- Tabs are placed by the watcher that lives in the chosen profile. CDP never guesses through 'the profile used last'.
- Nothing is hidden: the 'controlled by automated test software' bar and the Allow prompt stay. The app never auto-clicks, never starts the user's browser by itself, and never types passwords.

1. New module browsers.py (pure, testable on the Mac for any OS, like platforms.py)
- KNOWN table. Each row: id, display name, mac app paths, mac data dir, Windows exe paths, Windows data dir, inspect scheme, supported flag.
  - Supported in v1: brave, brave-beta, brave-nightly, chrome, chrome-beta, chrome-dev, chrome-canary, chromium.
  - Listed but not offered until verified: edge (+beta/dev/canary), arc, vivaldi. Opera is not listed: its profile layout differs.
- installed() -> list[Installed]
  - macOS: the .app exists in /Applications or ~/Applications, and its Info.plist CFBundleIdentifier matches. Don't use mdfind (it returned nothing here). Don't use the data folder alone (leftover folders exist here).
  - Windows: in this order:
    1. per-machine and per-user Application folders (%ProgramFiles%, %ProgramFiles(x86)%, %LOCALAPPDATA%);
    2. HKCU, then HKLM, SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\App Paths\<exe>;
    3. HKLM/HKCU SOFTWARE\Clients\StartMenuInternet\*\shell\open\command (also WOW6432Node), which is Windows' own list of registered browsers.
- os_default() -> id | None. It is used only to preselect a browser the first time.
  - macOS: LaunchServices secure plist, LSHandlers with scheme https, LSHandlerRoleAll. Here it is com.brave.browser.
  - Windows: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\Associations\UrlAssociations\https\UserChoice\ProgId (BraveHTML, ChromeHTML, MSEdgeHTM, …).
- profiles(user_data_dir) -> list[Profile(folder, name, color, is_ephemeral, signed_in: bool)]
  - Read from 'Local State' profile.info_cache, ordered by profile.profiles_order.
  - Drop 'System Profile', 'Guest Profile' and is_ephemeral entries.
  - color comes from profile_highlight_color, a signed ARGB int converted to #rrggbb.
  - user_name and gaia_name are never returned (they can be emails). signed_in is just a bool.
  - Tolerant: a missing or half-written file gives [].
- watcher_folders(user_data_dir, watcher_ids) -> {profile_folder: extension_id}
  - Reads '<profile>/Secure Preferences', then 'Preferences', looking at extensions.settings.<id>.
  - Counts an id only when it is one of the app's watcher ids and its disable_reasons list is empty.
- state(user_data_dir) -> 'not_installed' | 'not_running' | 'switch_off' | 'switch_on'
  - running: SingletonLock -> 'host-pid' with platforms.pid_alive(pid). On Windows: 'User Data\lockfile' cannot be opened because it is held (verify on the laptop).
  - switch_on: the existing chrome.switch_on (DevToolsActivePort plus TCP). Both files go stale after exit (measured), so both checks are needed.
- chrome.py keeps own_browser_dirs, find_ws_url and the launch() guard. The guard refuses every KNOWN data dir, not just Brave's and Chrome's.
  - own_browser_dir() order: AIB_CHROME_DIR, then the saved setting, then the first supported instance whose switch is on, then the OS default, then the first installed.
  - Claude Code sessions resolve it once per connection and remember it, instead of calling it again per message (engine.py:291-292).
  - browser_name() and inspect_address() come from the KNOWN row (brave://, chrome://, edge://inspect/#remote-debugging), not from 'bravesoftware' in the path.

2. The saved choice
- File: <home>/settings.json, written atomically: {"agents_browser": {"id": "brave", "user_data_dir": "...", "profile": "Default"}}.
- The first run preselects from os_default(), here Brave. The profile is the one holding the watcher, else Local State's last_used.
- The app passes AIB_CHROME_DIR and a new AIB_CHROME_PROFILE (the folder name) in each agent's env when the agent is created (extends run.py:105-107). So a later switch never moves a running agent.
- A Claude Code session reads settings.json when it connects.

3. Opening a tab in the chosen profile (replaces grouping.Placer.create_params' CDP-only path)
- With the app running and the chosen profile's watcher connected:
  1. The engine sends POST /agent-open {marker} through AgentLink.
  2. The app sends {type: 'open_tab', marker, key, title, color} to that profile's watcher.
  3. The watcher calls chrome.windows.getLastFocused({windowTypes:['normal']}), then chrome.tabs.create({url: 'about:blank#aib-<marker>', active: false, windowId}), and groups the tab in the same step.
  4. The engine waits up to about 2 s for Target.targetCreated whose url equals the marker, then attaches. The tab is 'owned', not 'adopted'.
  - Measured: this lands in the watcher's profile whatever profile was used last, with no focus change.
  - Private windows are excluded by construction: a watcher not allowed in incognito never sees them.
  - Popups from the agent's pages stay with their opener's profile (Chromium behaviour; a measured window.open landed in the opener's profile).
- Without the app (a lone Claude Code session), or with the watcher missing in that profile:
  - Context-less createTarget, as today. Then read TargetInfo.browserContextId and say honestly where the tab went, in the status line: 'opened in the profile you used last in Brave; load the watcher in <name> to pin agents there'.
  - Later tabs of that session pass browserContextId equal to the first tab's context. It works while that profile is the last-used one. On 'Failed to find browser context', the tab opens context-less and the result says so.
  - No userGesture popups and no focus tricks.
- Mapping a profile to its runtime context: the app looks for the watcher's service_worker target (chrome-extension://<watcher id>/worker.js) in the instance's target list, using the app's one connection, and reads its browserContextId.
  - If the watcher is loaded in two profiles under one id, the two can't be told apart. So each profile the user enables gets its own watcher copy in a different folder: <home>/app/watcher/<slug>. A different folder gives a different extension id, which watcher_folders() maps back to the profile folder. Today's single watcher keeps working as the copy for whichever profile Secure Preferences says has it.
- AI Home's tab list (bravelink.tabs, app/tabs.py) keeps browserContextId.
  - It lists only the chosen profile's context, plus the contexts of tabs agents own or were handed.
  - Other profiles show as one line, 'N tabs in other profiles', with no titles. Private-window tabs are never listed.

4. Settings: 'Where agents browse', in the approved app window
- A row of browser cards for each installed supported browser: name and icon glyph (generic), a state chip (switch on / switch off / not running / connected), and its profile count.
  - Detected but unsupported browsers show greyed with 'not supported yet'.
  - A card whose switch is off expands the three steps with that browser's own inspect address, plus the existing warning sentences from setup.html:84-90, parameterized by browser name.
- Under the selected browser, the profile list from Local State: colour dot, initials, name; '✓ watcher' or 'needs the watcher (one-time: Show me how)'; and the number of running agents in it.
- Copy under the list:
  - 'Switching profile in Brave needs no new Allow.'
  - 'Switching to another browser: it asks "Allow remote debugging?" once when you switch, and again for each agent while each agent still connects on its own.'
- Saving writes settings.json and sends 'browser_changed' to AI Home. The browser card, the tab list and the next agent's env all follow.

5. Quick switcher in AI Home
- The browser card header becomes a chip: '<Brave> · <Personal> ▾'. Its menu:
  - (a) profiles of the current browser. One click, instant, no prompt. A profile without its watcher shows 'needs the watcher' and links to Settings.
  - (b) the other installed supported browsers, each with its state. A browser whose switch is on reads 'Switch: Chrome will ask Allow once'. One whose switch is off reads 'Show me how'.
  - (c) 'Settings…'.
- A one-line notice follows a switch: 'New agents use Chrome · Work. 2 running agents stay in Brave · Personal.'
- Each agent row in AI Home and Mission Control gets a small place chip when it differs from the current default.

6. Running agents on a switch
- Running agents keep their instance and profile, pinned by their env and the context of their first tab. Their tabs, groups, Watch, Hand over and Take back keep working.
- Profile switch, same instance: the app's one connection stays. The tab list re-filters, and new agents and sessions use the new profile.
- Browser switch: the switch click is the user's action, so the app connects to the new instance right away. The card shows 'waiting for Allow' for up to 60 s (BraveLink states, bravelink.py:30).
  - The old instance's link stays open only while one of its agents is alive, and is dropped when the last one closes. At app start only the default instance is connected.
  - BraveLink becomes InstanceLink, one per user-data-dir.
- No 'move agent' exists, because cookies and logins differ per profile. Instead, an agent whose place differs from the default offers 'Restart in Chrome · Work', which starts a new agent with the same task text after the user clicks.
- Hand over: 'Give to <agent>' lists only agents in the same browser instance. Agents in another profile carry the label 'in <profile>'. A handed tab's group is made by its own profile's watcher, if any.
- Claude Code sessions keep their browser until their process restarts.

7. Consent per instance
- Each instance has its own switch, its own Allow, and its own state machine (off · ready · asking · connected · refused · lost).
- Connections happen only after a user action: app start (default only), Connect or Try again, a switch click, or an agent starting a turn. Detection never connects.
- Never connect to an instance the user didn't pick or that hosts no running agent.
- The 'turn it off when agents aren't working' advice and the bar sentence are shown per instance. Nothing hides the bar or the prompt.
- Fewer prompts per agent depends on the separate relay work (one connection per instance owned by the app). This design is compatible with it: profile choice adds no connections.

8. Windows and macOS paths (data dir ↔ install)
- Brave
  - macOS: data ~/Library/Application Support/BraveSoftware/Brave-Browser (-Beta, -Nightly); app /Applications/Brave Browser.app (com.brave.Browser, .beta, .nightly).
  - Windows: data %LOCALAPPDATA%\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data (Brave-Browser-Beta, Brave-Browser-Nightly); exe <root>\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\Application\brave.exe.
- Chrome
  - macOS: data ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome (Chrome Beta, Chrome Dev, Chrome Canary); app 'Google Chrome.app' (com.google.Chrome, .beta, .dev, .canary).
  - Windows: data %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data (Chrome Beta, Chrome Dev, and 'Chrome SxS' for Canary); exe <root>\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe (Canary installs per-user under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome SxS\Application).
- Chromium
  - macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Chromium (org.chromium.Chromium).
  - Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Chromium\User Data.
- Edge (unverified, not offered)
  - macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Microsoft Edge (Edge Beta/Dev/Canary), com.microsoft.edgemac.
  - Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Edge\User Data (Edge Beta, Edge Dev, Edge SxS); msedge.exe under %ProgramFiles(x86)%\Microsoft\Edge\Application.
- Arc (not supported)
  - macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Arc/User Data.
  - Windows: an MSIX package under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\TheBrowserCompany.Arc_*\LocalCache\Local\Arc\User Data (unverified).
- On Windows, DevToolsActivePort and 'Local State' sit in 'User Data'. Profiles are User Data\Default and User Data\Profile N, each with 'Secure Preferences'. The running check uses 'User Data\lockfile'.
- Paths are compared with realpath plus ntpath.normcase (chrome.py:133-138).
- All of this goes in platforms.py (guard 3 keeps macOS literals there).

9. Tests (no real browsers)
- Two-profile tests must be headful throwaway Chrome. Measured: headless ignored the second --profile-directory and never created 'Profile 2'.
- Use fixture Local State and Secure Preferences JSON for profiles() and watcher_folders().
- Use a temp folder with DevToolsActivePort plus a local socket, and a SingletonLock symlink, for state().
- The marker open_tab flow uses a throwaway extension in one profile, as in probe4.

Probe scripts, all against throwaway browsers: /private/tmp/claude-501/profile-probe/probe.py, probe2.py, probe3.py (Brave), probe4.py (extension in one profile), probe5.py (private window).
risks: The watcher becomes the only exact way to put a tab in a chosen profile. Without the app, or without the watcher in that profile, tabs fall back to Brave's last-used profile. This is said honestly, but it is not fixed.
Telling profiles apart needs one watcher copy per profile (a different folder gives a different extension id). That is an extra one-time 'Load unpacked' per profile the user wants agents in.

Secure Preferences and Local State are Chromium internals, not an API. Field names were measured on Chrome 154 and Brave 152 and could change. Every read must tolerate failure and fall back to 'unknown', never crash or guess.
Local State is complete only after the browser writes it, often at exit, so a just-created profile may be missing from the list until Brave flushes it.
Local State holds emails in user_name and gaia_name. These must never reach AI Home rows, the Brain's state summary, or Claude.

A future Chromium may list real profiles in getBrowserContexts. createTarget with a browserContextId would then work directly. Keep the verify-after-create check, so behaviour stays correct either way.

Edge's and Arc's support for the chrome://inspect remote-debugging switch is unverified. Windows' 'User Data\lockfile' running check and the Windows paths for Beta, Canary and Arc need a manual check on the laptop.

When the chosen profile has no open window, the watcher can't open a tab without creating a window. chrome.windows.create({focused:false}) may still draw the user's eye, and if the profile isn't loaded at all there is no watcher to ask.
On a browser switch with agents still running, two instances are connected at once. That means two 'controlled by automated software' bars and two connections reachable while both switches are on.
AI Home's current tab list leaks titles of private-window and other-profile tabs (app/tabs.py:65-69). This should be fixed even if the rest of this design waits.
open_questions_for_user: Your Brave has two profiles (Default and Profile 1). Which one should agents use: the one where you're signed in to the sites they need, or the one where the Brain's watcher already is? They can differ, but then you load the watcher in both, once each.

When the chosen profile has no Brave window open, may AI Browser open a window for it when you click a button? That launches Brave with that profile and brings it to the front. Or should it only tell you to open that profile yourself?
When you switch browsers while agents are still working, should they keep working in the old browser until they finish (my proposal), or stop?
Which browsers should Settings offer at first: just Brave and Google Chrome (including Beta and Canary), or Microsoft Edge too, once checked?
Should AI Home's tab list show only the agents' profile, with other profiles as a count and private windows never shown (my proposal), or every profile of that browser?

About the Brain: should it get a 'send to an existing agent' action? It would show a card 'Send to <agent>: …' that you confirm, instead of always starting a new agent. And should handing that agent a tab be offered in the same step?

design:
GOAL: The chat beside the page moves into the watcher, in the user's everyday browser. It becomes the one place to talk to existing agents, hand them the tab you are on, and answer their cards. It adds no new debugging connection: it uses only the app's 127.0.0.1 WebSocket. It needs no `debugger` permission (spec Decision 5 stands) and no new host permission.

1. MANIFEST AND OPENING (watcher/manifest.json)
- Add "sidePanel" to permissions (no install warning) and "side_panel": {"default_path": "panel.html"}.
- Add the commands._execute_action shortcut (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Y, as in extension/manifest.json:13-18).
- In worker.js call chrome.sidePanel.setPanelBehavior({openPanelOnActionClick: true}), so the toolbar icon opens the chat. The Brain page moves behind an 'Inbox' button in the panel header (it uses openBrain() as today).
- Setup tells the user to pin the watcher icon, because Brave has no sidebar entry for extension panels (brave#31334).
- Use one panel per window, never per-tab panels.
- Call sidePanel.open() only from a click inside an extension page, and only after checking chrome.windows.get(id).type === "normal" (avoids the crash in brave#59256).
- A notification's Review button keeps opening the Brain page. Whether a notification click counts as a gesture for sidePanel.open is not measured, so it is not relied on.

2. WHICH TAB THE CHAT IS BESIDE
- The panel takes its own window with chrome.windows.getCurrent() (measured: it works in the panel). It follows only that window's active tab: tabs.onActivated filtered by windowId, plus tabs.onUpdated for that tab. This replaces lastFocusedWindow (panel.js:102), so each window's panel stays put.
- The panel knows tab.id, windowId, url and title (the `tabs` permission already exists). It never knows target ids.
- The server stops sending `tabs` and `thumbs` to watcher-origin sockets.
- Layout, top to bottom:
  (a) A TAB STRIP describing the tab beside the panel: 'This tab: mail.google.com · yours', or '· handed to Blue', or '· Blue's tab', or 'a browser page'.
  (b) THE CONVERSATION.
  (c) THE COMPOSER, with an explicit 'To:' picker listing existing agents (newest first, with state dots), 'New agent', and nothing else.
- The conversation shown is the picker's choice. It defaults to the owner of the beside tab when that is known; otherwise it keeps the last choice, so switching tabs does not throw away the conversation the user is in.
- This is the fix for the Brain complaint: telling an existing agent something is choosing it in To: and pressing Enter (`send {id, text}`). The Brain does not interpret it. A new agent appears in To: at once, so it can always be messaged again.
- OWNERSHIP:
  - The server keeps a map of everyday-browser tab id to owner. It fills it from grouping answers (GroupKeeper.remember, groups.py:74-78) and from the panel's own hand-overs.
  - It pushes `tab_owners {browser, owners: {tabId: {kind, id, name, color}}}` to watcher-origin sockets of that browser.
  - A tab missing from the map shows as 'yours'. If it really belongs to an agent, the server refuses any hand-over and the strip corrects itself from the reply.

3. MAPPING TO TARGET IDS, HANDED TABS AND HAND OVER (all resolved on the server)
- The panel sends a tab descriptor, never a target: {id, window, url, title}.
- The server resolves it with resolve_tab(desc):
  1. If the tab id is in the map and the target still exists with the same url, use it.
  2. Otherwise take the candidates from BraveLink.tabs() whose url equals desc.url.
  3. If there is one, use it. If there are several, keep those whose new BraveLink.window_of(target) equals desc.window. window_of calls CDP Browser.getWindowForTarget, a browser-level call that never attaches to the user's tab, so the promise in bravelink.py:1-8 holds.
  4. Still several means 'ambiguous': refuse with 'Two tabs in this window show this page: close one, or hand it over from the app's tab list'. None means 'changed': refuse with 'The page changed, click again'. It never guesses (groups.js:74).
  5. On success, remember the tab id to target pair (GroupKeeper.remember) and re-check _handable (owner you or brain, server.py:497-504).
- New messages, all from the panel, all needing a trusted click (event.isTrusted in the handler):
  - `start_here {text, model, request, tab}`: a new agent created with adopt = the resolved target, owner and group set as in server.py:692-694.
  - `hand_here {id, tab}`: calls _hand(id, target) (server.py:511-523), the panel version of AI Home's Hand over.
  - `take_back_here {tab}`: calls agents.take_back(target) plus _own(target, None).
  - Replies: `hand_result {request, ok, reason}`.
- If BraveLink is not connected, start_here and hand_here come right after the user's click, so the server may call connect_brave(). Brave then asks 'Allow remote debugging?', which follows the spec's 'only right after something the user did'. Nothing hides or answers that prompt.
- STARTING IN THE CURRENT TAB IS A HAND-OVER AND NEEDS A CLICK:
  - On a tab that is 'yours' with To: New agent, Send is split into two buttons: '[Start here · mail.google.com]' (primary, a hand-over) and '[Start in its own tabs]'.
  - Enter does nothing until one of them is clicked, and the hint says 'Choose where it works'.
  - With To: an existing agent, Enter sends the message. A separate button, '[Hand this tab to Blue]', hands the tab over; typing never does.
  - On a handed tab the strip shows '[Take back]'.
- The panel never sends the beside tab's url or title to an agent unless that tab is handed to it. `send` carries tab {}, and handed tabs reach the agent through HANDED_NOTE and page_line(label "handed") as today (agents.py:24, bridge.py:66-75).

4. PERMISSION AND CHECK CARDS IN THE PANEL
- Reuse permission.js, already shared. The shown agent's card sits above the composer, as in panel.js:83-88.
- A line 'Green and 1 more agent are waiting for you' switches To: to that agent. It never answers anything.
- In the watcher the card offers Allow once and Deny. Always allow becomes a link, 'Always allow is in the app's Tools', and the server refuses answer:"always" from the watcher origin. This is an open question below; today the Brain page in Brave can Always allow.
- Bot checks: add check.js to WATCHER_SHARED with an option skip:false. It shows 'To skip it, tell the agent: skip it' (check.js:27), Show me and Continue.
  - Show me activates the tab locally with chrome.tabs.update when its tab id is known; otherwise it sends `watch {target}`.
  - Continue sends check_continue, which is already allowed. The panel never touches the check.
- chat.js is shared too. Everything is rendered with textContent only, as now (chat.js:5-22).
- The composer button is labelled 'Tell' or 'Start', not 'Send', so it is not mistaken for a site's Send.

5. TRUST MODEL: AN EXPLICIT PER-ORIGIN ALLOWLIST (replaces the deny-list in server.py:644-673)
- The server cannot verify which watcher page sent a message (all share one origin and the hello view is self-declared), so privilege is per origin.
- WATCHER ORIGIN MAY:
  - Reports: hello, items, replied, thread, filled, reader_status, watcher_caps, tab_grouped.
  - Brain inbox, unchanged: brain, draft, approve, done, tell, hand, workflow_run only with an `item`, watch_set, watch_remove, pause, style.
  - Agents: events; new_task without adopt (the agent works in its own background tabs); send; stop; model.
  - Tabs: start_here, hand_here and take_back_here (tab descriptor, resolved on the server, only for a watcher in the agents' browser); watch.
  - Cards: permission with once or deny; check_continue.
- WATCHER ORIGIN MAY NOT:
  - new_task with adopt (refuse it: fixes the gap measured today); hand_tab or take_back with raw targets; brave_connect.
  - check_skip; close (ending agents stays in the app window); permission with always.
  - tools, tool_set, tool_allow, tool_forget; workflow_save, workflow_delete, workflow_run without an item; skill_draft, skill_save; skills.
  - Hearing and voice; brain_ask, brain_confirm, brain_dismiss (no talk with the Brain in phase 1).
  - Receiving `tabs`, `thumbs` or target ids beyond its own handed and agent tabs.
- App origin: everything, as today.
- Implementation: replace the elif chain's origin tests with ROLE_ALLOW = {"app": ALL, "watcher": WATCHER_ALLOWED}, checked once at the top of _handle; unlisted messages are dropped silently. Extend tests/test_app_server.py:737 into a table test covering every message type for each origin.
- The panel page registers no chrome.runtime.onMessage listener, so content scripts cannot reach it. The panel's CSP stays the MV3 default and nothing is web_accessible.
- READING AND DRAFTING STAY AS THEY ARE. SEND STILL NEVER HAPPENS FROM THE WATCHER:
  - fill_reply only fills the box, and test_watcher.py:176 keeps enforcing it.
  - Agents the panel starts can press a site's Send only through the ⚠ gate after the user agrees (bridge.py:41, browser.py:36,62). That is the same as agents started anywhere; the panel only makes handing a tab easier, which is why it takes a click and names the host.

6. THE WATCHER'S PROMISE TEXT (new wording)
- manifest.json:5: "The Brain's inbox and your agents' chat, beside your tabs. It never sends a message for you; agents get a tab only when you hand it over."
- brain.html:26: "(only tabs you have open; it reads and drafts, and you press Send)".
- setup.html:61-62 and README.md:217,243: "It reads new messages, drafts replies you approve, and shows your agents' chat beside your tabs. It never sends anything itself: you press Send. An agent works in one of your tabs only after you click Start here or Hand over, and it asks you before any ⚠ step like Send, Buy or Delete."
- The panel's first-run line says the same in one sentence.
- worker.js:1-4: update the header comment.

7. CHROME AS WELL AS BRAVE: ONE EXTENSION ID PER BROWSER
- prepare_watcher writes two folders, <home>/app/watcher (Brave) and <home>/app/watcher-chrome (Chrome). Each folder gets a distinct ID (the ID is the SHA-256 of the path), and each gets a generated browser.js (export const BROWSER = "brave" | "chrome"), next to build.js.
- run.py allows both origins, each with its browser: allow_origin(origin, watcher="brave"|"chrome").
- hello carries the browser. The worker checks navigator.userAgentData.brands (measured: 'Brave' in Brave, 'Google Chrome' in Chrome) and refuses to connect when the copy is in the wrong browser. It then shows a badge and a note: 'This copy is for Brave; in Chrome load watcher-chrome'.
- The server keeps _watchers[browser] in place of the single slot (server.py:638):
  - group_tab, ungroup_tabs and the panel's tab resolution use only the watcher of the browser the agents drive (the 'Default browser in Settings' choice).
  - open_thread and fill_reply go to the browser whose reader reported that item.
  - Notifications go to the agents' browser's watcher, so they are not doubled.
- In the other browser the panel is chat and cards only. Start here and Hand are disabled with 'Agents work in Brave. Switch the default browser in Settings to work in this tab.'
- setup.html gets a Chrome step (chrome://extensions, Load unpacked, the second folder) with /reveal?which=watcher-chrome.
- Multiple profiles of one browser share an ID, and the panel's resolution works across them because window ids are process-wide. Grouping should later go to every watcher of that browser, with the first ok winning.

8. PHASES AND EFFORT (about 6-8 developer days)
- P0, 0.5-1 d: the per-origin allowlist and the new_task.adopt refusal, plus table tests. Worth doing even if the panel never moves.
- P1, 3-4 d: the watcher panel (adapt panel.html/js/css; To: picker, tab strip, split Start buttons, cards); shared chat.js and check.js; start_here, hand_here, take_back_here and tab_owners on the server; BraveLink.window_of; promise text; CDP tests in a throwaway Brave or Chrome, as in tests/test_panel.py.
- P2, 1.5-2 d: the Chrome copy (two folders and IDs, per-browser watcher slots, setup page).
- P3, 0.5 d: retire extension/panel.* and the 'debugger'/'sidePanel' parts of AI Browser's extension once the approved app window exists.
- Plus about 0.5 d of hand checks in the user's Brave: toolbar opening, a popup window, notification gesture behaviour.
risks: Brave side-panel bugs: Brave crashes when an extension opens a side panel for a tab in a popup window (brave#59256, open, filed 2026-09-22 on 1.95.10x). Mitigation: only open() for windows of type 'normal', and prefer openPanelOnActionClick. 1.95 has not been measured; 1.94.121 worked in the probe.

Brave has no sidebar entry for extension panels (brave#31334), so finding the chat depends on the user pinning the watcher's toolbar icon or using the shortcut. Brave's own sidebar column may also take width next to the panel (brave#51271).

Matching tabs to targets without debugger is not exact. The same address twice in one window is refused ('ambiguous'). A single-page app that changes its address between the click and the server's check (for example Gmail's #hash) is refused and needs a second click. This is a small loss compared with today's chrome.debugger.getTargets (extension/link.js:70-84), which spec Decision 5 rejected for the watcher on purpose.

Wrong-browser hand-over: if a Chrome copy and a Brave copy shared one origin, a click in Chrome on gmail could be resolved to the Brave tab showing the same address. The per-browser IDs, the hello check and the server rule 'resolve only for the agents' browser's watcher' are what prevent it. Do not ship the Chrome copy before them.

Trust expansion: the everyday-browser extension that sits next to Gmail and Slack readers gains the power to start agents in the user's logged-in tabs. A bug that turns page data into a command would now matter more. Mitigations: an explicit allowlist, server-side resolution with _handable re-checks, trusted-click-only hand-overs, no runtime.onMessage in the panel, and textContent everywhere.

The existing gap measured today, new_task with adopt and tool_allow accepted from the watcher origin, should be closed (P0) before the watcher gains a UI that sends new_task. Otherwise the deny-list gets wider without anyone noticing.

Changing the promise: users who installed the watcher under 'never sends anything' get new powers when the watcher reloads itself (worker.js:86-92). The sidePanel permission shows no warning, so nothing in Brave tells them. The new wording should be shown once in the panel and on the Brain page.

Several Brave profiles share the watcher's ID, and the server keeps only the latest watcher (server.py:638). Grouping, thread and notification messages can go to a profile that doesn't hold the tab ('not_found'). The panel's own resolution is unaffected, because window ids are process-wide.
Duplicate notifications when both the Chrome and the Brave watchers are connected, unless notifications go only to the agents' browser's watcher.

Not measured: whether clicking the toolbar icon with openPanelOnActionClick works in Brave 1.94 (the probe opened the panel from a click inside a page, not from the icon), and whether a notification button click counts as a gesture for sidePanel.open.
open_questions_for_user: On one of your own tabs, should pressing Enter in the chat ever start an agent in that tab? I recommend no: you choose between two buttons, 'Start here · <site>' (hands the tab over) and 'Start in its own tabs', and Enter waits until you pick.

Should 'Always allow' for a tool be offered in the chat inside your everyday browser? I recommend no: only 'Allow once' and 'Deny' there, with 'Always allow' kept in the app's Tools. Today the Brain page in Brave can still 'Always allow'.

Should the side chat also talk to the Brain (typed only, no mic)? Or should it address agents directly with a 'To:' picker, so delegating to an existing agent is a click rather than the Brain's guess? I recommend agents only for now. The Brain would need a new 'message this agent' card before it can delegate.

Do you want the watcher in Google Chrome too? It means loading a second folder once in chrome://extensions. In whichever browser the agents aren't using, the chat can talk and answer cards but can't hand over that browser's tabs.
When you hand over a tab of a site the Brain watches (Gmail, Slack, Asana), should there be an extra line to confirm, such as 'The agent will be able to act in your inbox'?
You open several Brave profiles: should the watcher, and so the chat, be loaded in all of them, or only in the one you work in?

title: Brain delegating to an existing agent

findings.point: Nothing in the talk path can start an agent unless the user confirms it, so this is not a safety bypass. The proposal set really is closed to start_agent and draft_reply. respond() only ever creates a proposal, and only confirm() creates an agent. confirm() runs from a Start click (brain_confirm) or from a plain yes to the matching open card. Talk messages from the watcher's origin are refused.
findings.evidence: src/ai_browser/brain/service.py:601-643 (respond only proposes: :631-633, :634-641); :645-662 (confirm is the only agents.create, :650-653, after talks.take closes the card first, :647); src/ai_browser/brain/talk.py:303-321 (one proposal per talk, runs once); src/ai_browser/app/server.py:58, :671-673, :799-821.

findings.point: Bug 1 (root cause): the Brain has no way to message an existing agent. Its prompt says that any request for work must become start_agent. So 'tell/give this to the footer agent' can only become a card that starts a NEW agent. If Claude tries to message the agent instead (message_agent, send, delegate), the reply is CLICK_ONLY, 'I can't approve, send, allow or delete anything', which gives the wrong reason. That is why the user 'cannot command it back' by talking.
findings.evidence: talk.py:19 ACTIONS = (none, start_agent, draft_reply, open); talk.py:40-46 (TALK: 'When the user asks for work, propose one action: start_agent … or draft_reply'); talk.py:159-160 (an unknown action string gives CLICK_ONLY). Probe /private/tmp/claude-501/brain-delegate-probe/probe.py, case 2: message_agent, send and delegate all give CLICK_ONLY. tests/test_brain_talk.py:86-87 pins 'send' to CLICK_ONLY.

findings.point: Bug 2: a card's spoken 'say' is Claude's free text and is never checked against the card. Claude can say 'Sure, I'll pass that to the footer agent' while the card starts a new agent. The answer is spoken aloud, and a plain 'Okay.' or 'Sure' to the open card runs it with no Claude call. This is the most likely way a yes-like word confirmed the new agent the user didn't want.
findings.evidence: service.py:628 reply = {"say": parsed.say} and talk.py:175 (say passes through for start_agent). talk.py:31-32: YES includes ok, okay, sure, go ahead, do it. talk.js:476-480 attaches the open card's id to every brain_ask, and service.py:606-610 runs confirm on is_yes. Probe case 1: say 'Sure, I'll pass that to the footer agent.', then 'Okay.' gave created=['tell the footer agent to also check the mobile layout'] and sent_to_existing=[].

findings.point: Bug 3: a card's task is only the user's latest words. After a clarifying exchange, the card's task becomes the answer to the clarifying question ('the footer one'). After a yes with no card open, the task becomes 'yes'.
findings.evidence: service.py:632 task=text and :640 guidance=text, the current utterance only. Probe case 3: the card task was 'the footer one'. Probe case 4: with no card open, 'yes' went to Claude, which proposed start_agent with task 'yes'.

findings.point: What the Brain knows about agents: for the 20 newest, only id (a1, a2…), name (the first words of the task), state (needs_you when a permission or bot check waits), doing (status or last action), and labels for a waiting permission or bot check. It gets no colour, no number the user can see, no tabs (working, opened or handed), no model and no queued messages. It also doesn't know which agent the talk last dealt with. So 'agent 2', 'the blue one' or 'it' cannot be resolved reliably, and the user never sees ids anyway: Mission Control shows only names and colour dots.
findings.evidence: talk.py:92-102 (_agent), :114-125 (state_data). The fields that exist but are never passed on: agents.py:76-78 Agent.PUBLIC has color, tabs, adopted, working_tab, model. mission.js:109-127 (List row: dot + name + state); scene.js:189 (nameplate = name); agents.py:147 (name = _name(task), colour cycles through 7).

findings.point: Why the spawned agent said the user must provide the tab. In Brave mode agents get BRAVE_PROMPT: they may use only tabs they open and tabs the user hands them. The engine refuses to adopt any tab that wasn't handed over, and with no tab it answers 'switch to a tab the user handed you'. The new agent's task talked about another agent's or the user's page, which it may not see or list. So asking for the tab was correct. But nothing tells the user where Hand over is. It exists only in AI Home's tab list, not in Mission Control where the talk lives. And the prompt doesn't suggest the alternative: opening the address in the agent's own tab, which is in the user's Brave profile with their logins.

findings.point: Agents can already be messaged by click: Mission Control's drawer has a composer, and AgentManager.send queues for a busy agent and records a 'queued' event. The Brain never routes to it or mentions it. The voice-input spec deliberately left 'talking to one agent … and Hand to agent proposals' for later, 'with the same confirm rule'.

TELL has no 'existing agent' choice, so typing 'give this to the footer agent' there spawns a new agent. (b) A workflow set to run right away, when a message arrives. (c) The address bar's 'ai <task>'.
